label: AQ 0020
title: The team built for one shape

questions.q: Anthropic's multi-agent system beat a single agent by 90.2%. Doesn't that contradict you?
questions.a: No. That was research: broad searching that splits into independent threads, at about 15 times the tokens of a chat. Anthropic itself says work needing shared context or many dependencies between agents isn't a good fit, and most coding tasks have fewer parallel parts.

teach.title: How it works: why the team breaks, and when it doesn't

questions.q: Can't better handoff summaries fix it?
questions.a: Partly. Cognition's rule is to share “full agent traces, not just individual messages”, because actions carry hidden decisions. But even perfect notes don't give a fixed PM → coder → tester line a way back from the tester to the planner. That needs replanning.

teach.title: How it works: why the team breaks, and when it doesn't

questions.q: How do you keep the tester's viewpoint with one agent?
questions.a: Ask the same agent to review its own diff as a strict tester, then run the real tests. The role costs a prompt; a separate agent costs a context boundary, and the tests are the outside check either way.

teach.title: How it works: why the team breaks, and when it doesn't

questions.q: What are MAST's three groups of multi-agent failures?
questions.a: System design issues, misalignment between agents, and task verification. The MAST study found 14 failure modes in over 1,600 traces from 7 frameworks; the most common was step repetition at 15.7%.

teach.title: How it works: why the team breaks, and when it doesn't

questions.q: Why doesn't MAGIS's eight-fold gain prove that role teams beat one agent?
questions.a: Its baseline was GPT-4 applied directly to SWE-bench issues, which I read as one model call with no loop or tools, not a well-run single agent.

teach.title: How it works: why the team breaks, and when it doesn't

questions.q: Give two signs that a coding task should stay with one agent.
questions.a: The subtasks share state, such as edits to the same files, and the plan may need to change mid-task when tests reveal something. Anthropic names many dependencies between agents as a poor fit for multi-agent systems.
